description: we are students intersted in building solutions using human intelligence
summary: A 3D recreation of the planet Mars, built on real NASA data from Viking, MOLA, HiRISE, THEMIS, TES and Curiosity, where you can explore, navigate, simulate, find and save your new explorations and discoveries. Plan a walk, check every slope, dust field and temperature on the way, and know before you step outside how much oxygen, cooling water and battery each crew member will have left. All with an approach that puts safety above everything else
details:
What it does

Mars View is a 3D Mars you can plan a walk on. We chose one real place, the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp that Curiosity explored in 2025, and asked what an astronaut would ask before stepping outside: will I make it back?

The globe shows real NASA data, each layer with its source: Viking and HiRISE images, MOLA and HRSC elevation, THEMIS and TES thermal maps, a dust map, and Curiosity's latest weather.

You drop a few stops and the planner finds a path the suit can handle, avoiding steep slopes, rough ground and soft dust, and explaining every detour. Then it counts oxygen, cooling water and battery for each person in a crew of two. If anyone would return with less than 20%, the plan is refused with the reason, like "Crew B runs out of oxygen 2.05 km out."

Why it matters

Existing maps show whole regions. An astronaut needs their walk. Mars View turns NASA data into one clear answer: go or don't go, and why.

How we built it

JavaScript, CesiumJS for the 3D globe, Three.js and WebXR for VR, and a small Node.js server for elevation and map tiles. The planner is a variant of A*. Survival numbers come from Apollo moonwalk data and the Apollo 15–17 backpacks; anything assumed is labelled.

What makes it creative

It's a decision tool, not just a map. It has 14 one-click scenarios (a leaking suit, a canyon wall, a walk too far on foot but fine for a rover), a guided tutorial, a 360° VR walk through Jezero, and signed data files that the app refuses to use if a single byte changes.

What we considered

Safety first: a 20% reserve and a clear "no" with a reason. Honesty: terrain is 200 m to 2.6 km per pixel, so routes are a plan, not a guarantee, and Mars has no weather forecast, so we show measured weather. Teamwork: a crew of two, where the weaker budget decides.
